newsitem.title: FRANCE: French markets seen nervous after shock poll result.
newsitem.headline: French markets seen nervous after shock poll result.

text.p: French financial markets are expected to react nervously after left-wing parties took an unexpectedly strong lead in the first round of National Assembly elections on Sunday, traders and economists said.

A pall of uncertainty will keep investors on their toes until after the June 1 second round, they added, while doubts over the Socialists stance towards European Monetary Union (EMU) could hit the Italian lira and the Spanish peseta.

International factors, such as Friday's 1.2 percent gains by Wall Street stocks, could give support to the French financial markets while the closure of U.S. and British markets on Monday could mute the international market reaction.
"The market will be disapppointed, the numbers are worse than expected for the right-wing coalition," said Michelle Jardin, equities strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.

"We could see a downside correction (in the share market) in the area of five percent next week. Even though the decisive results will be after next week's poll, the market will be nervous," she added.
"The franc is weakening and obviously the markets should open much lower tomorrow morning," said Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance.

"One problem for the market reaction is that London and New York will be closed on Monday so the market will be a bit odd. The Anglo-Saxon investors may sell more aggressively so there may be another wave of selling on Tuesday," he added.
Before the first-round projections came in from 1800 GMT, the franc had been trading at 3.712/3.716 against the German mark. After the results it slipped to 3.720/25.
Brossard saw the franc slipping to 3.3800 or 3.3850 against the mark on Monday.

He added the French election result could be negative for the Italian lira and the Spanish peseta as well because a Socialist government is expected to be less strict on economic convergence for the EMU.

"It is pretty much as bad as it could get, we do not know who will win the second round and what this could mean for the final number. The markets would rather have not seen the left and the National Front achieving this performance," said economist Marie Owens-Thomsen at bank BIP.

"It does look as if the left could actually win, but the Socialists moved very much toward the centre in the last days of the campaign so that choosing them was like choosing between sides of a mirror," she said.

"The stock market risks selling off more than the bond market...The bond market sold off quite significantly on Thursday and Friday, I think we have a more realistic level in the bond market," she said.
The French CAC-40 blue-chip stock index gained 0.78 percent to 2,762.90 on Friday, close to its all-time high of 2.771.48.

"This is definitely bad news for the markets. We could see a two percent correction tomorrow, but I would be surprised if it was more, said Elisabetta Castelli, head of international equity sales at the CDC bank.

"The left has not so far shown it has a credible programme, it has not embraced market economics in the way the current U.K. government has. It is talking about undoing privatisations, it poses a question over Maastricht. This is a setback for corporate governance in France," she added.
